title: Copying solos note for note: Trumbauer, Armstrong and Hawkins
summary: His first copied solo was Trumbauer's Singin' the Blues; there were few alto models, and Hawkins invented tenor style.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: Uh huh. What about in this early stage. You know, many musicians, as they describe their development, began by -- I was gonna say 'merely' or 'simply', but that's not really quite the word -- but began by copying note for note, solos of musicians that they admired. And many, many musicians recount how they had done this in the formative stages.

The first solo that I copied, apropos of what you're saying now, was Frankie Trumbauer's 'Singing the Blues' -- ba da dee dee doo -- note for note, you know, so you're quite right there, and I remember how all the trumpet players used to play Louis Armstrong's 'Chinatown' and that was a big thing, you know - that was like in the early twenties, oh, '24, '25 -- or whenever.
And the Dipper Mouth. That, too ... yes, yes.

Yes, that's right. But I certainly did copy note for note, "Singin' the Blues" -- I don't know what else I copied, note for note. There wasn't just that much of alto players that I was interested in to copy, you know?
This is what I was gonna get at, too, that there just weren't that many models around.

See, there was Coleman Hawkins with his tenor playing, and he was pretty hard to copy because he had something going for himself, you know --the same thing applied. There weren't too many tenor players to whom he could've listen, to whom he could've patterned his style after. So he really created something, I feel.

But I would make the claim, at least until somewhat later, that your playing -- in terms of just the mechanics, or the approach to the instrument -- was much more advanced than his during the period which you were together early in the Henderson band. His phrasing, still, I think, is still much rougher. That slap tongue effect.
I don't know ... it sounded awful good
then. And everything he played since then sounded awfully good, too. Jesus. I don't know.
